transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose what brought me in is that I just keep getting up in meetings or at dinner when everyone else is seated. Like, I'll suddenly feel the need to refill my coffee or go check a handout. I teach secondary school, you know, and we just got these new curriculum handouts from the district. Honestly, they are so poorly formatted. The font is incredibly tiny, and they used this glossy paper that just glares under the fluorescent lights in my classroom. I brought it up to the principal, but you know how administration is, they just nod and do absolutely nothing about it. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, getting up. Yes, I'll just suddenly stand up and walk to the back of the room during a staff meeting, or pop up from the dinner table, even though nothing is actually urgent. My husband finally suggested I should probably come talk to someone about it.
Did you experience similar difficulty sitting still or staying seated when you were a child?

Oh, absolutely. Even as a girl, my report cards always said the same thing—that I was bright but could not stay in my seat or wait my turn. My mother used to joke that I wore a path between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was ten. Speaking of pencils, do you remember those old crank sharpeners they used to have bolted to the wall in classrooms? The ones that smelled like cedar shavings? We had one in my fourth-grade class, Mrs. Gable's room. She was a lovely woman, wore these bright floral dresses every day, but she was so strict about margins on our lined paper. I still think about her when I'm grading my own students' essays. They don't even use pencils anymore, it's all typed on tablets now. The school gave them all these cheap little tablets last year, and the screens crack if you just look at them wrong. I must have had to send three kids to the IT office just this week because their screens were shattered. 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, being a child. Yes, always up and about, never could just sit still at my desk.
Do you often find it hard to maintain your focus on tasks or make careless mistakes at work or home?

Careless mistakes? No, I wouldn't say that. I'm actually quite meticulous, especially with my grading. You really have to be, otherwise the students will argue with you over every single half-point. I always use a purple pen for grading now—they told us at a professional development seminar a few years ago that red ink is too aggressive and damages the students' self-esteem. Can you imagine? Red ink being aggressive. 

Anyway, I used to get these absolutely wonderful Japanese gel pens from a little stationery shop downtown. It was such a lovely store, smelled just like fresh paper and binding glue. But they closed down during the pandemic, which was just a tragedy. It’s an artisanal bakery now. They do make a very nice sourdough, I have to admit. My husband picked up a loaf just this past Saturday and we made the most incredible grilled cheese sandwiches with this sharp cheddar we found at the farmer's market... 

Oh, dear, I'm doing it again, aren't I? What was the question? Focus! Right. No, my focus is perfectly fine, and I don't really make careless errors. I just can't seem to stay in my chair.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient demonstrates pervasive signs of hyperactivity and motor restlessness, including repeatedly leaving her seat when expected to remain seated and marked tangential, excessive speech. These behaviors have been consistently present since early childhood (prior to age 10) across multiple settings (workplace meetings and home). She explicitly denies inattentive symptoms such as making careless mistakes or poor task focus, establishing a presentation consistent with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, predominantly hyperactive/impulsive presentation (F90.1).
